# HQ

> HQ is the company brain your AI runs on. It keeps a company's knowledge, projects, skills, workflows, credentials and AI teammates in one shared system the company owns, and it works across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, ChatGPT and Claude. The core is open source (MIT).

Key facts:

- What it is: a suite of six connected products (HQ Core, HQ Cloud, Secrets + Integrations, HQ Deploy, HQ Bots, HQ MCP) that gives a company one way to work with AI. It does not replace AI tools or models. It gives them shared company context, tools and access.
- Who it's for: companies and teams that want everyone, technical or not, working from the same AI context. Common users are founders and operators, agencies running many client workspaces, and consumer brands. Nontechnical teammates usually use HQ through Claude Desktop or ChatGPT (via HQ MCP), Slack, email, or deployed apps. A smaller operator group installs HQ and builds skills.
- Pricing: sign up free with $10 of usage included every month and a 30-day free trial covering up to $500 of usage. After that, pay as you go. No seat fees. Deploys, DMs and background AI are free. Hosted AI agents run on boxes billed monthly by size, from $100 to $800. Enterprise is priced by contract. Full rates: https://hqforwork.com/pricing
- Free self-hosted option: the open-source HQ core and the HQ CLI run on your own machines with no HQ account and no cloud.
- Install: download the desktop app for macOS or Windows at https://hqforwork.com/install, or run `npx create-hq` in a terminal. A Linux desktop app is on a waitlist.
- Data: local-first. Company memory lives in ordinary files in the HQ workspace. When HQ Cloud is used, synced data is encrypted in transit and at rest, credentials get separate field-level encryption, and each company is an isolated tenant.
- Official domains: hqforwork.com (product site) and docs.hq.computer (documentation). Source code: https://github.com/indigoai-us/hq-core

This file is the full text of the main pages on hqforwork.com: products, pricing, install and getting started, FAQ, use cases, case studies, and services. For a short index, see https://hqforwork.com/llms.txt

# Products

## HQ Products: The AI Operating System for companies

Source: https://hqforwork.com/products

> HQ gives companies persistent AI memory, shared capabilities, secure connections, deployable work, and AI teammates in one operating system.

#### Built for how your company actually works.

Each product solves a real problem teams hit with AI, all on one shared memory.

##### HQ Core

File-based company memory, loaded into every AI session.

##### HQ Cloud

Your entire HQ, kept in sync across the team and every device.

##### HQ Secrets + Integrations

Connect systems once. Credentials stay encrypted in HQ.

##### HQ Deploy

Ship finished work as live links with access control built in.

##### HQ Bots

Persistent Bots with roles, memory, and their own inbox.

##### HQ MCP

Company memory and tools, served to any AI over MCP.

## HQ Core: The file-based memory system and harness for AI

Source: https://hqforwork.com/products/core

> HQ Core is an open-source, file-based memory system and harness that gives AI your company’s Knowledge, Skills, Projects, Workers, and Policies.

#### Company memory you can see, own, and improve.

Most AI memory is trapped inside one conversation or one vendor. HQ Core is different: it is a durable, file-based system for the knowledge, instructions, active work, specialists, and rules that make your company yours.

Because the memory is made of files, people can browse it, edit it, share it, and understand exactly what the AI is using. It becomes company infrastructure instead of hidden chat history.

#### Store the company once. Bring the right pieces into every session.

##### Memory lives in files

Knowledge, Skills, Projects, Workers, and Policies give the company a clear, durable structure.

##### The harness loads it

HQ identifies the company and work at hand, then gives the AI the relevant memory, capabilities, and rules.

##### The system compounds

Work creates new decisions, handoffs, and reusable ways of working that become available to future sessions and teammates.

#### Everything your AI needs to know how you work.

##### Knowledge

The decisions, documents, and context your company relies on.

##### Skills

Repeatable ways to do your company’s best work.

##### Projects

Shared goals, plans, and work in progress.

##### Workers

Specialists your AI can call when the work needs them.

##### Policies

The rules and guardrails that keep work consistent.

## HQ Cloud: Sync and share HQ with your whole team

Source: https://hqforwork.com/products/cloud

> HQ Cloud manages the syncing, sharing, visibility, and access that keeps your company’s HQ current across the whole team.

#### HQ should not live on one person’s computer.

HQ Core creates the company’s memory and operating structure. HQ Cloud turns it into a shared system the whole team can use, rather than a collection of files and connections that only one person has.

It keeps the important parts of HQ current across people and computers, gives administrators one Console for visibility and access, and lets teammates share the same company context without passing folders or credentials around.

#### The memory, capabilities, and access behind the work.

##### Company memory

Knowledge, Projects, Policies, and the shared files that give AI company context.

##### Skills + Workers

The repeatable ways of working and reusable specialists the team has built.

##### MCP + connections

The Integrations and Secrets that connect HQ to the systems the company uses.

##### People + access

The teammates, Bots, groups, and grants that decide who can use each part of HQ.

#### Keep every approved piece of HQ current.

HQ Sync keeps local and cloud HQ aligned across the team. Updates to company memory, Skills, Projects, Workers, Policies, and other approved files move to the people who have access, while conflicts surface for review instead of silently overwriting someone’s work.

## HQ Secrets + Integrations: One universal company connection

Source: https://hqforwork.com/products/integrations

> Connect every company system to HQ once, protect its credentials, and provision reusable access to teammates and HQ Bots.

#### The company needs one connection layer, not another pile of keys.

Useful work depends on data sources, communication tools, customer systems, internal services, and custom MCP servers. Connecting each one separately in every AI tool creates duplicate setup and credentials nobody can safely govern.

HQ becomes the universal connection layer. Systems connect to HQ once, credentials stay protected in Secrets, and the company provisions reusable access to the teammates and Bots who need it.

#### Turn every company system into a reusable HQ connection.

##### Connect

Add a service, integration, or custom MCP server to the company’s HQ.

##### Protect

Store the credential in HQ Secrets instead of a prompt, document, message, or local setup.

##### Provision

Choose which teammates, groups, and Bots can use the connection without distributing the raw credential.

##### Use

Approved connections become available through HQ sessions, Bots, Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI tools.

##### Keep it working

Sign-ins expire and services go down. HQ records what happened to a connection and names the reason in plain language. When the fix is a credential or a setting, it says who can make it — the person who set it up, or a company owner. When the service itself is down, it says that too, rather than sending someone to fix what is not theirs.

#### Connect it once. Make it available to everyone who needs it.

Use people, groups, and Bot identities to provision access. A teammate can use the company connection through HQ without setting it up again, and a Bot can do its job without ever receiving the underlying key. Sharing reflects reality: a connection that has stopped working says so next to the people it is shared with, rather than quietly promising four teammates access to something none of them can use.

## HQ Deploy: Share what AI makes

Source: https://hqforwork.com/products/deploy

> Turn AI-made reports, dashboards, portals, and lightweight apps into polished links your team, clients, or customers can open.

#### Finished AI work should be easy for other people to use.

AI can create a report, dashboard, portal, or lightweight app, but the result often remains trapped in a local folder, development server, or conversation.

HQ Deploy handles the step between “the AI finished it” and “other people can use it,” without requiring the person doing the work to become a hosting expert.

#### Go from a local artifact to a useful link.

When the work is ready, HQ Deploy publishes it without making you stop to set up hosting or infrastructure.

##### Create

Build the report, dashboard, portal, or app inside an AI work session.

##### Deploy

HQ packages and publishes the finished artifact, then returns a live URL.

##### Share

Send one polished link instead of source files, setup instructions, or a local preview.

#### Open to everyone, or only the right people.

Share a public link, add password protection, or require authenticated company access for private reports, portals, and internal tools.

## HQ Bots: AI teammates that show up for work

Source: https://hqforwork.com/products/bots

> HQ Bots are persistent AI employees and company teammates with Slack, email, memory, tools, and ongoing responsibilities.

#### Some work needs a teammate, not another chat.

A chat waits for someone to open it, explain the task, and keep the conversation moving. That works for one-off requests, but it does not create ownership.

Each HQ Bot has an identity, responsibilities, company context, and approved tools. It can keep continuity across requests and own work that continues over time.

#### Give the Bot a role and a place on the team.

##### Define the teammate

Give the Bot a name, role, responsibilities, and the company or team it belongs to.

##### Give it context

The Bot receives the relevant HQ memory, policies, Skills, and approved connections it needs.

##### Put it to work

Teammates can reach it in Slack, by email, or through direct assignments.

##### Let it initiate

The Bot can also begin work when a schedule or company event calls for it.

#### They work where your team works.

##### In Slack

Message a Bot in a channel or thread, bring it into conversations, and keep the work visible to the team.

##### Over email

Every Bot receives an email address, so it can receive requests, reply, and take part in the workflows that already run through the inbox.

## HQ MCP: Bring HQ to Claude, ChatGPT, and every AI tool

Source: https://hqforwork.com/products/mcp

> Bring company memory, tools, Secrets, and Integrations into Claude and ChatGPT through one permissioned HQ MCP connection.

#### Use Chat when Chat is the right interface.

HQ Bots can own ongoing work, but many people still prefer a direct conversation for research, writing, analysis, or a one-off task. They should not have to adopt a Bot workflow to benefit from HQ.

HQ MCP gives Claude and ChatGPT a shared, permissioned connection to the company. People keep the chat interface they already know while HQ supplies the memory, tools, and systems underneath.

#### Connect the chat. Ask with company context.

##### Connect

Add one HQ MCP connection to Claude or ChatGPT.

##### Bring the company

The chat can reach the company memory, Skills, tools, and systems that person is allowed to use.

##### Stay in the conversation

The AI can find context and take action through approved connections without the person leaving Chat.

#### The chats your team already uses. Now with your HQ.

Give Claude and ChatGPT access to the same company memory and capabilities your team uses everywhere else.

##### Claude

Bring company context and HQ capabilities directly into Claude conversations.

##### ChatGPT

Find and use company knowledge without leaving ChatGPT.

#### What usage costs

The first $10 of usage every month is included. Past that you pay for what you use at these rates.
| Service | What counts | Price |
| Sync | Each sync that moves changed files | $0.10 per sync |
| Gateway call | A connected app or outside MCP call through HQ | $0.05 per call |
| HQ MCP call | A call to HQ's own MCP tools | $0.05 per call |
| Agent run | One run of a hosted AI agent | $0.05 per run |
| Storage | Files kept in HQ, including old versions | $2 per GB per month |
| Secret | Each API key or password kept in HQ | $0.50 per secret per month |
| Vault | Each company and personal vault, waived in the trial | $5 per vault per month |

##### Hosted AI agents

Each hosted agent runs on its own box, billed monthly by size.
| Box | Instance | Price |
| Small | t3.small | $100 per month |
| Medium | t3.medium | $200 per month |
| Large | t3.large | $400 per month |
| XLarge | t3.xlarge | $800 per month |
- Deploys, DMs and background AI are free. Bots you run on your own computer have no box fee.
- Custom domains: $20 per month each, or $500 per month for a company-wide domain.

#### Common questions

**Q:** How does pricing work?

Sign up free and get $10 of usage included every month. New accounts also start with a 30-day free trial that covers up to $500 of usage. After that you pay as you go at the rates above. There are no seat fees, and deploys, DMs and background AI are free.

**Q:** What is the vault fee?

Each company vault and each personal vault is $5 per month. It is billed as usage, so the $10 included each month covers it, and it is waived during the trial.

**Q:** What does a hosted AI agent cost?

Each hosted agent runs on its own box, billed monthly by size: small (t3.small) $100, medium (t3.medium) $200, large (t3.large) $400, xlarge (t3.xlarge) $800. Bots you run on your own computer have no box fee.

**Q:** Can I run HQ without the cloud?

Yes. Run the open-source HQ core (MIT license) and the HQ CLI on your own machines, with no HQ account and no cloud. Your files stay on your hardware. Advanced, enterprise and government teams can run it self-hosted or on-prem. The guide linked above shows how.

**Q:** What does guided setup include?

We set HQ up with your team: a setup call with an HQ expert, your tools and knowledge connected for you, agents built around how your team works, and team training, plus SSO and dedicated servers if you need them. Book a setup call and we scope it with you. The call is free.

**Q:** I am already on an HQ plan. Does it change?

No. Your current plan and prices stay as they are.

**Q:** Can I cancel?

Yes, at any time. Usage is billed monthly.

Billed monthly in US dollars, with a live meter and budget caps. No seat fees. Cancel anytime.

# Install and getting started

## Install HQ — Get AI out of the chat box

Source: https://hqforwork.com/install

> Download HQ for macOS or Windows and get set up in minutes. Signed on both platforms, or bootstrap from the terminal with npx create-hq.

Install

### Get AI out of the chat box.

Download HQ, open it, and you’re minutes from AI that works beside you on your real work. Signed on macOS and Windows. On macOS it runs with no Gatekeeper warnings; on Windows you may need to click past a SmartScreen or antivirus prompt.

Why install it

#### It’s the difference between using AI and wielding it.

Prefer the terminal?

#### Skip the installer. One command.

Bootstrap HQ straight from your shell — same result, no download.

### bootstrap HQ from your shell — one command:

Once it’s installed

#### From download to building.

The same setup we’d walk you through in a session — start to finish, on your own.

Favorites
- AirDrop
- Recents
- Applications
- Downloads

// 01

Open the installer

Once it downloads, open it. It’s signed with HQ’s Apple Developer ID and notarized by Apple, so there are no Gatekeeper warnings.

// 02

Log in and launch

Step through to the end and sign in with your email - the one you were invited to your company’s team with, if that applies. Then click the white “Launch in Claude Code” button.

// 03

Trust your workspace

Claude Code will open with your hq folder selected and /setup ready to run. Choose “Yes, trust this workspace.” Just check that hq is still the folder it’s pointing at (~/hq).

// 04

Dial in your settings

For the best results, use the latest models (Opus 4.8 or GPT-5.5), set thinking to “High” or above, and turn on auto mode (bypass permissions). You might need to flip that last one on in settings.

// 05

Press enter to run /setup

Hit ⏎ in the message box to start setup.

// 06

Answer, then run /handoff

Work through every question until it says setup is finished, then send “/handoff” to save everything to HQ’s memory. You’ll do this at the end of every session.

// 07

Open a fresh session and build

Start with “/brainstorm” to get going. Working on a specific company? Send “/startwork acme” and describe what you want to do. Then it’s the same rhythm every time: start work, handoff, repeat.

##### Open the installer

##### Log in and launch

##### Trust your workspace

##### Dial in your settings

##### Press enter to run /setup

##### Answer, then run /handoff

##### Open a fresh session and build

Continue with the course

Rather have a guided hand than go it alone? Grab a time and we’ll get you building in your very first session.

## Your First 30 Minutes: What Setup Does · HQ Knowledge Hub

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/setup

> Anyone who just installed HQ and is about to run setup, or is mid-setup and wondering what's happening.

**Q:** All articles

**Q:** On this page

Illustrative · the one-time setup interview, about 20 minutes

#### The one thing to know before you start

Almost nothing in setup is mandatory. The one step you can't skip is connecting a coding tool (Claude Code or Codex), because your HQ assistant runs on it. Everything else can be skipped and setup still completes. Say "skip" to anything else, anytime. The social questions are optional, and you can add everything later.

Setup is the one-time conversation that turns a freshly installed HQ folder into your HQ. There are two ways to start it:
- In the HQ app (most people). After install, click the HQ Desktop card on the HQ is ready. screen. HQ Desktop opens a short guided setup of up to seven screens:
- Name your HQ assistant.
- Your team ("Who do you work with?"): join the company that invited you, Start a company, or Just me.
- Your coding tools: sign in to Claude Code or Codex. One is enough, and this is the step that can't be skipped. If a tool isn't installed yet, Install Claude Code (or Install Codex) installs it for you.
- Bring in your context: click Bring it in so your assistant learns your companies, projects, and people from this computer. It reads only this computer, and nothing leaves it. Or click Skip for now.
- Note taker: connect Fireflies, Otter, or Read.ai.
- Project management: connect Linear.
- Done: a summary and a Talk to button with your assistant's name.

Screens 5 and 6 only show up when you're setting up with a company, and you can click Next to skip them. From the context screen on, Continue in chat and Finish with defaults let you finish early. Your assistant then picks up the rest of setup in chat, starting at the first step you haven't done, without re-asking what you already answered. See Installing HQ on macOS or Installing HQ on Windows.
- In Claude Code or Codex directly. If you already use one of them, open your HQ folder in it and type:

Both run the same setup. The rest of this page covers what it does, phase by phase.

One quick disambiguation, because these three commands (the short instructions you type into Claude Code or Codex) get confused constantly: /setup = your HQ, run once. /onboard = create or join a company (an isolated workspace for one business or team). /accept = redeem an invite link someone sent you. If you were invited to a team, you still run setup first.

#### Phase 1: Health check and self-repair

Setup first checks the record the HQ app left behind during install, a list of every install step, including any that failed. If something didn't land (a tool didn't download, the search index didn't build), setup explains what's missing in one sentence, fixes it, and checks the fix before moving on.

This is why "the install showed an error" is almost never a reinstall situation. Setup repairs it.

What it feels like: a short checklist scrolling by, with the occasional "want me to install this?" question.

#### Phase 2: Your team

You already signed in to HQ with Google or Microsoft when you installed the app. Setup just confirms you're signed in to HQ Cloud, and if you aren't, opens a browser window so you can. It never blocks setup on this. Signing in is what turns on team sync (keeping your HQ current across machines and teammates), shared companies, and publishing your work behind a link.

If a teammate invited you, your team's company appears automatically as long as you signed in with the email address the invite went to. If you were sent an invite link instead, /accept with the link redeems it.

In the HQ app, guided setup asks "Who do you work with?" You can join the company that invited you, Start a company, or pick Just me. To invite teammates, ask your assistant. It asks for each person's email and whether they're a member or an admin, confirms, then sends the invite. Tell them to check their spam folder if it doesn't arrive in a few minutes. A new or joined company syncs to your computer by itself. If a company invite arrives later, accept it from the Notifications bell in the top bar of the HQ app.

#### Phase 3: Five questions about you

Setup asks five questions, one at a time:
- Your name.
- What you do.
- Your goals for HQ: what you want AI help with.
- Your biggest pain points: what's slow, repetitive, or keeps slipping.
- Your systems of record: where your work's truth lives (CRM, spreadsheets, email, a database, Slack…), and whether each has a credential you could connect later. You're never asked for a password or key here, only whether one exists.

These are worth answering well, and here's why: your answers become the standing context every future work session (one sitting of work with the AI) starts with. Name a real pain point, like "I lose two hours every Monday rebuilding the pipeline report," and everything downstream gets sharper. Setup's suggestions target that exact task, and future sessions attack it without being re-briefed. Vague answers ("be more productive") get you vague help. Two minutes of honesty here pays off for months.

Setup may also offer to look at your public profiles (LinkedIn, X, a personal site) to learn your voice, and (if you've used Claude Code before HQ) offer to import your existing skills, plans, and projects with /import-context (the old name, /import-claude, still works). Both optional, both skippable.

In the HQ app, your assistant can also connect the apps you use, one at a time, with your okay for each. After the first one works, it says something like "Great, Fireflies is connected" and links to your integrations page on hq.computer, where you can see everything that's connected. You can ask it, or any other AI in HQ, to connect another one later.

#### Phase 4: Your HQ folder takes shape

Setup now scaffolds your workspace. No action needed from you. But it's worth knowing what exists when it's done:
- personal/: your private overlay. It holds your profile, preferences, and any skills (packaged, reusable workflows) or notes that belong to you rather than to a company. Inside it, personal/knowledge/ holds your knowledge base (the searchable notes HQ consults so it never has to re-ask): your profile, your systems-of-record list, and your voice notes.
- repos/: the single home for any code or content repositories you bring in later, split into public/ and private/.
- Profile files that HQ reads at the start of every session so it always knows who it's working for and what to prioritize.

#### Phase 5: The 60-second orientation

Before finishing, setup gives you the HQ mental model in a screenful: sessions are disposable and context is precious (start with /startwork, do one focused thing, end with /handoff, the command that saves your state for next time); everything lives in one of three homes (personal/, companies/, repos/); knowledge compounds; and slash commands are how you drive. It also points you at /tutorial, a set of hands-on lessons you can take anytime. Deeper dive: mental-model.md.

Your assistant in the HQ app keeps this in plain words and doesn't ask you to type commands. The habit it teaches is simple: when you finish working in Claude Code or Codex, ask it to wrap up the session, so the next one picks up where you left off.

#### Phase 6: "Dream big," then a concrete launch plan

Setup closes with two things:
- Two or three tailored scenarios built from your answers: "you said X eats your time; here's the HQ capability that attacks it," so you can see the destination, not just the tooling.
- A short interview about what you need first, ending in a personal launch plan: a list of exact commands to run next, each with a one-line reason tied to your goals. This plan is saved to personal/knowledge/getting-started-next-steps.md, so you can close everything and find it again tomorrow.

Setup also publishes a small private welcome page, your profile, your setup summary, and your launch plan as copy-paste blocks, and gives you the link.

#### What to do next

Close the setup session (fresh sessions are an HQ habit, and a good one), open a new one, and go get a real result on the board. That's the single most important move after setup. Half of new users stall right here, and the cure is shipping one small, real thing.

Go to your-first-win.md. It gives you three copy-paste-ready first projects, with exact commands, what HQ will ask, and what "done" looks like.

#### Common questions

**Q:** I skipped a bunch of phases. Did I break anything?

No. As long as a coding tool is connected, setup completes. Rerun the pieces later: /personal-interview to deepen your profile, /import-context to import prior Claude Code, Codex, Grok, and claude.ai work.

**Q:** Do the identity answers get shared anywhere?

They're written into your local HQ folder (your personal/ area). They're for your AI's context, not for publication. Only the optional welcome page is published, and it's private to you.

**Q:** Setup mentioned invites but I don't see my team's company.

Check that you signed in to the HQ app with the email address the invite went to. Invites tied to your email are claimed when HQ syncs, and a company you join syncs to your computer by itself. If the company still doesn't appear, look for an Added to banner with your company's name in the HQ window and click Sync now. It only appears if that automatic sync failed. You can also right-click the HQ icon in your menu bar (Mac) or system tray (Windows) and choose Sync Now, or run /hq-sync. If you were sent a magic link instead, redeem it with /accept followed by the link. See team-rollout.md.

**Q:** What's the difference between /setup and /onboard again?

/setup = your HQ, once, ever. /onboard = create or join a company. /accept <invite> = shortcut for joining via an invite link.

#### If you get stuck

If setup halts on a broken dependency, just tell it "skip" and keep going. You can repair later by running setup again (it only fixes what's missing; it won't clobber your answers). For anything weirder, see im-stuck.md or file it with /hq-bug.

## HQ Cloud: What It Is and Whether You Need It · HQ Knowledge Hub

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/cloud

> Anyone deciding whether to connect HQ to the cloud, solo users, team members, and team leads alike.

**Q:** All articles

**Q:** On this page

Cloud is what you add the day teammates enter the picture

Here is the most important thing to know, stated up front: HQ works fully on its own, offline, with no account and no cloud. Everything core to HQ, your projects, your knowledge base (the organized notes and context HQ builds up about your work), your skills (the reusable instructions behind HQ's commands), your daily workflow, lives in a folder on your computer and runs there.

HQ Cloud is what you add when you want more than a solo setup: syncing between machines, sharing with teammates, safely storing passwords and API keys, and turning your meetings into searchable notes. If you never sign in, nothing breaks. If the answer to "do I work with other people in HQ?" is no, you may not need this article yet.

#### The pieces of HQ Cloud, in plain English

Each cloud feature is optional and does one job:

Login and identity. Signing in tells HQ Cloud who you are. You run /hq-login once (it opens your browser to sign in), /hq-whoami any time you want to check who you're signed in as, and /hq-logout to sign out. One login powers everything else on this list.

The vault. Every cloud-backed company (a company in HQ is an isolated workspace for one business or team) gets its own encrypted online storage space, called the vault. It is the "cloud copy" of that company's files. You can browse it without downloading everything using /hq-files.

Sync. Sync keeps the files on your laptop and the files in the vault matched, in both directions, for every cloud-backed company (one whose files are connected to a vault). It runs automatically in the HQ app, or on demand with /hq-sync. This is how your teammate's new notes appear on your machine, and how your work appears on theirs. Full details in the sync guide.

Share links. /hq-share lets you share a file or folder from the vault, either as a single-use encrypted link (it expires after 15 minutes) or as a durable grant to a specific person or group. See Sharing your work.

Direct messages. /dm sends a message straight to a teammate's HQ app, where it shows up under Direct messages, optionally with a ready-to-use prompt their own HQ can act on, or a scheduled delivery time. You can even DM yourself as a reminder.

Secrets. An encrypted store for API keys and passwords, so HQ can use your tools without you ever pasting a credential into a chat. Covered fully in the secrets guide.

Deploy. /deploy publishes something HQ made for you, a report, a webpage, a dashboard, to a link you can send to anyone. See Sharing your work.

Meeting intelligence. A meeting bot that joins your calls, transcribes them, and extracts action items and decisions. See Meeting notes and signals.

#### Do I need cloud? A quick decision guide

If you're an Operator (everyday user, not living in a terminal):

You need cloud if your team already uses HQ together, sign in so you receive the shared knowledge, messages, and files. If you're using HQ alone on one computer, you can skip cloud entirely and add it later. Nothing you do now gets lost.

If you're a Builder (technical user):

Cloud earns its keep the moment you (a) work from two machines, (b) need secrets injected into commands without keeping them in plain-text .env files, or (c) want to hand teammates a working setup instead of a README. Solo on one machine with your own secret management? Optional.

If you're a Champion (rolling HQ out to a team):

You need cloud, it is the mechanism that makes HQ a team system rather than a personal one. Shared companies, invites, roles, synced knowledge, and meeting intelligence all ride on it. Start with the team rollout guide.

#### What goes to the cloud, and what stays on your machine

Being honest about this matters, so here is the actual split:

Goes to the cloud (only after you sign in and opt in):
- Files inside cloud-backed companies. When a company is designated cloud-backed, the files under its folder sync to that company's encrypted vault so teammates can receive them. Companies you never cloud-back never sync.
- Anything you explicitly share or deploy with /hq-share or /deploy.
- Secrets you store, which live encrypted in the cloud vault (and never appear in chat). Secret names and metadata are visible to you in listings; values stay encrypted and are only injected into commands you run.
- Direct messages, which are stored server-side for delivery, so don't put secrets in a DM.
- Meeting recordings and transcripts, if you invite the meeting bot to calls, processing happens on HQ cloud.

Private to you (not shared with your team):
- Your sessions, the raw conversations you have with HQ stay on your machine and aren't uploaded.
- Your workspace and handoffs, drafts, session state, and handoff threads sync to your own private personal scope, so they follow you to your other machines, but your team doesn't see them.
- Your personal overlay, the personal/ folder (your private settings and notes) also syncs to that personal scope, which is auto-provisioned when you sign in and on by default.
- Everything, if you never sign in. Solo, offline HQ sends nothing anywhere.

Each company's vault is isolated from every other company's. HQ treats keeping companies separate as a hard rule, so one team's knowledge never leaks into another's.

#### Common questions

**Q:** Can I use HQ solo, without the cloud, forever?

Yes. Solo and offline is a fully supported way to run HQ, not a trial mode. Cloud is additive.

**Q:** If I sign in, does everything upload automatically?

No. Signing in by itself uploads nothing. Files only sync for companies that have been explicitly made cloud-backed (usually by your team lead with /designate-team).

**Q:** Can I start solo and add cloud later?

Yes, and it's a common path. Run /hq-login when you're ready; nothing about your local setup has to change first.

**Q:** Is there a separate cloud app?

HQ is one app that installs your HQ folder and then keeps syncing from your menu bar (Mac) or system tray (Windows). If HQ isn't running, see the sync guide troubleshooting section.

#### If you get stuck

The most common cloud issue is simply not being signed in, run /hq-whoami to check, and /hq-login to fix. For sync problems, go to the sync guide; for anything else, the "I'm stuck" guide or /hq-bug to report it to the team.

## Sessions, Checkpoints, and Handoffs · HQ Knowledge Hub

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/sessions

> Anyone whose sessions get long, slow, or die mid-task, which is everyone, eventually.

**Q:** All articles

**Q:** On this page

Illustrative · sessions are disposable, the handoff is forever

A session is one conversation with your AI assistant. This article covers the habit that makes HQ feel reliable instead of forgetful: end sessions on purpose, and start fresh ones often.

#### Why fresh sessions beat one long session

Every session has a limited working memory (a "context window"). As a conversation grows, that window fills with everything said and every file read. Two things then happen:
- Quality degrades. A crowded memory means the assistant starts overlooking earlier decisions and making sloppier choices.
- Eventually the session dies. Past the hard limit, the session simply can't continue ("Prompt is too long").

HQ's answer is not "try to keep sessions alive", it's the opposite. Sessions are disposable; the files HQ writes between sessions are what persist. A fresh session that reads a good handoff is sharper than an old session limping along, because it has all the conclusions and none of the clutter. (This is the heart of the HQ mental model.)

#### The arc: /startwork → work → /handoff

1. Start with /startwork. At the top of a session, this command orients you: if a previous handoff exists, it offers to resume it (showing a one-line summary of where you left off); otherwise it asks what you want to work on, a company, a project, a repo, or a free-form task, and loads just the context that choice needs.

2. Work. Do the actual thing.

3. End with /handoff. This writes a "thread", a structured record with a summary of what happened, the next steps, the files touched, the git state, and any learnings, then commits everything so nothing is lost. It finishes by printing a thread ID and telling you exactly how to continue:
- In your next session, run /resumework {thread-id} to continue that exact piece of work, or
- Run /startwork and pick "Resume last session".

When you resume, HQ also lists next steps left open by your recent handoffs, so nothing falls through the cracks between sessions. Steps are marked done as you finish them.

That's the whole daily loop.

#### /checkpoint, the mid-session save

/checkpoint is the lighter sibling of /handoff: a quick save of your progress (summary, files touched, next steps, git state) without ending the session. Think of it like hitting Save in a document.

Use it during long sessions, especially before starting anything risky or large, so that even if the session dies later, your progress up to the checkpoint is recorded. If the session feels long enough that you're checkpointing repeatedly, that's your cue to /handoff instead.

#### /recover-session, when a session dies without a handoff

Sometimes a session hits the context limit and dies before you ran /handoff. Your work on disk is fine, you just lost the tidy summary. In a new session, run:

HQ scans the last 7 days for sessions that died at the context limit, shows you a list, and reconstructs a thread for the one you pick, what the session set out to do, which files it edited, and what it was doing when it died. From there you continue as if a handoff had been written. It never touches your git state, so nothing is committed without you.

#### Signs it's time to hand off
- The session has been running for hours or has covered several unrelated tasks.
- Responses are getting slower, or the assistant repeats itself or forgets earlier decisions.
- You're about to switch task types (e.g., from coding to writing marketing copy).
- You've finished a milestone, a natural chapter break.
- You see any warning about context or compaction.

When in doubt, hand off. It costs a minute; a degraded session costs much more.

#### Where handoff files live

Everything lands under workspace/threads/ inside your HQ folder:
- workspace/threads/T-{date}-{time}-{slug}.json, each thread (handoff, checkpoint, or recovered session).
- workspace/threads/handoff.json, a pointer to the most recent handoff; this is what /startwork peeks at.
- workspace/threads/recent.md, a human-readable table of your recent threads.
- Threads older than 60 days are archived into workspace/threads/archive/.

You never need to edit these by hand, the commands manage them, but it's useful to know they're plain files: searchable with /search, and synced between your machines when you use HQ Cloud.

#### Common questions

**Q:** Do I lose anything by ending a session?

Not if you /handoff first. Files, commits, and knowledge all live on disk; the handoff captures the working state (what's done, what's next) that would otherwise exist only in the conversation.

**Q:** What's the difference between /handoff and /checkpoint?

/checkpoint is a quick save mid-session; /handoff is the full end-of-session package (richer record, learnings capture, commits, and a printed thread ID to resume from). Checkpoint and keep going; handoff and start fresh.

**Q:** What's the difference between /startwork and /resumework?

/startwork is the general session opener, it offers your latest handoff plus other options. /resumework {thread-id} jumps straight back into one specific thread, which is handy when you juggle several work streams.

**Q:** How often should I start a fresh session?

At minimum, one session per distinct task or work block. Many users hand off several times a day. Fresh is cheap.

#### If you get stuck

If a session died and /recover-session doesn't find it, it may have been too recent or too small to detect, check workspace/threads/recent.md for the last saved state, or just describe to a fresh session what you were doing. For anything else, see the I'm stuck guide or file /hq-bug.

## From Idea to Shipped · HQ Knowledge Hub

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/development

> Anyone with a project in mind who wants to know which planning command to use and how execution actually works.

**Q:** All articles

**Q:** On this page

Match the tool to the size of the thought

HQ turns ideas into shipped work through a planning ladder, four rungs from a ten-second note to a deep strategic plan, followed by execution commands that do the building. The most common mistake is starting on the wrong rung: over-planning a tiny idea, or under-planning a big one. This article gives you the sizing guide.

#### The planning ladder

##### Rung 1: /idea, capture a one-liner (10 seconds)

Got a thought you don't want to lose? Capture it:

That's it. HQ writes the idea to your company's board (a company is an isolated workspace for one business or team, and its knowledge never mixes with other companies'). No plan, no questions, no commitment. You can add --company acme if HQ can't tell which company it belongs to.

Use when: you want to remember it, not work on it yet.

##### Rung 2: /brainstorm, explore a fuzzy idea (a few minutes)

When you have an idea but aren't sure how (or whether) to build it:

HQ researches what your company already knows about the topic, challenges the premise ("is this even the right problem? what's the 80% solution?"), asks you at most one batch of questions, and writes a brainstorm.md comparing 2 to 3 approaches with tradeoffs and a clear recommendation. If you later promote it with /prd, the brainstorm pre-fills most of the interview.

Use when: the idea is fuzzy, there are multiple ways to do it, or you're not sure it's worth doing at all.

##### Rung 3: /prd, the standard plan (right for ~90% of projects)

This is the workhorse. HQ scans what it already knows (existing projects, relevant knowledge, your company's rules), then interviews you in short batches about the problem, who it's for, what's in and out of scope, quality checks, and how you'll know it works. It's the lightweight flow: a quick set of batched questions, faster still if a brainstorm already exists. For large or strategically important work, the heavier /deep-plan flow runs a longer, research-backed interview.

The output is a PRD. In plain English, that's a Product Requirements Document, the written plan HQ executes from. In HQ it's two files: prd.json (the machine-readable source of truth) and README.md (the human-readable view). Importantly, /prd only plans. It never starts building. Execution happens in a fresh session, on purpose.

Use when: you know what you want and it's more than a quick tweak. When in doubt, use /prd.

##### Rung 4: /deep-plan, big strategic work only

Everything /prd does, plus parallel research agents that study your codebase and company context first, and a deeper three-tier interview (strategic, architecture, quality, up to 15 questions). It costs more of your time up front, which is exactly right for work that's large, strategically important, or touches unfamiliar territory, and wrong for everything else.

Use when: getting it wrong would be expensive. Otherwise, /prd.

##### Sizing guide at a glance
| Your situation | Rung |
| "Don't want to forget this" | /idea |
| "Something here, but fuzzy; not sure how or whether" | /brainstorm |
| "I know what I want built" (≈90% of projects) | /prd |
| "Big, strategic, expensive to get wrong" | /deep-plan |

#### What's inside a PRD: stories and acceptance criteria

A PRD breaks the project into user stories: small pieces of work, each completable in one session, with IDs like US-001, US-002. Each story has acceptance criteria: the specific, checkable statements that define done, like "the calculator shows a price after selecting a plan and seat count."

Acceptance criteria are how HQ knows it's actually done. Vague criteria produce vague work. "Works correctly" is not a criterion; "submitting the form with an empty email shows a validation error" is. This checking pressure is what keeps autonomous execution honest, so it's worth being picky during the /prd interview.

#### Execution: one story or the whole plan

Once the PRD exists, start a fresh session (the plan even reminds you) and choose:

One story at a time with /execute-task:

Executes exactly one story: specialized workers (persistent AI specialists, like a backend builder, a reviewer, and so on) each handle their part, automated checks (tests, linting) verify the work, and the story is marked passed only when its acceptance criteria hold. Good when you want to review between steps.

The whole PRD on its own with /run-project:

Runs story after story on its own: shows you the plan, gets your approval, then works through every incomplete story with a fresh worker per story. This story-by-story rhythm (pick a task, plan, execute, verify, commit, next) is the Ralph Loop, HQ's core execution pattern. Add --dry-run to preview the story order without executing, or --status to check progress.

#### A worked example, end to end

Monday, in a meeting: someone mentions customers want a pricing calculator.

Tuesday, you have 20 minutes. You're not sure if it should live on the website or in the app:

HQ compares "embed on marketing site" vs "build into the app," recommends the marketing site as the narrower first step, and flags one unknown (where the price list lives). Looks right.

The interview is quick because the brainstorm pre-filled most answers. You confirm scope, name the non-goals ("no currency conversion"), and tighten the acceptance criteria. Out comes a PRD with five stories, US-001 through US-005.

Wednesday, fresh session:

You approve the plan; HQ works through the stories, verifying each against its criteria. Story US-004 fails its check the first time (the validation error didn't show), so it's fixed before moving on. When it's done: /deploy for a live link to share with the team (Sharing your work), and /handoff to close out (The daily loop).

#### Common questions

**Q:** Do I have to climb every rung?

No. Each rung is optional. Clear idea → straight to /prd. Most projects skip /idea and /brainstorm entirely.

**Q:** Can I edit the PRD after it's created?

Yes. The README.md is readable and the plan is yours. If you want a plan pressure-tested before executing, run /review-plan.

**Q:** Why won't /prd just start building?

By design. Planning and executing in the same session mixes contexts and skips HQ's tracking, worker assignment, and quality gates. The fresh-session rule is what makes execution reliable. See Sessions, checkpoints, and handoffs.

**Q:** /run-project or /execute-task: which should I default to?

/execute-task while you're learning or when the work is sensitive; /run-project once you trust the plan. Both verify every story the same way.

**Q:** Where do the files go?

companies/{company}/projects/{name}/. Plan, stories, and progress all live there. Find any project later with /search (Finding anything).

#### If you get stuck

If /run-project or /execute-task says the command isn't available, your install may be missing the engineering pack. The /prd output prints the one-line install command. For anything else, see The "I'm stuck" guide or file /hq-bug.

## Every HQ Command at a Glance · HQ Knowledge Hub

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/cheat-sheet

> Anyone who wants the full menu: every HQ command on one page, with a one-line purpose and a link to the article that teaches it.

**Q:** All articles

**Q:** On this page

A command is what you type inside a session, like /prd or /handoff. If you're not sure how commands relate to skills and workers, Commands, Skills, and Workers untangles it in six minutes. This page lists the commands that ship with a current HQ install, checked against the real command surface rather than older documentation.

Five things to know before the tables:
- The engineering commands are built in. Planning, testing, code review, debugging, and shipping commands like /tdd, /review, and /land now come with HQ itself, so there's nothing extra to install. A few other commands still arrive through capability packs, and those are tagged, for example (ships in hq-pack-email-assistant). If a tagged command is missing on your machine, the pack isn't installed yet. Capability Packs: Installing and Managing Them shows the two-minute fix.
- Commands with a company prefix, like acme:weekly-report, are skills your own team created. They're specific to your company, so they aren't listed here.
- If you read about a command elsewhere and it isn't on this page (for example /nexttask or /remember), it was probably renamed in a later release. The "I'm Stuck" Guide covers what to do when a command you expected doesn't exist.
- /plan is gone as of HQ 16. Use /prd with the same arguments. Skills also stopped reading CONTEXT.md. They read GLOSSARY.md (and GLOSSARY-MAP.md) now, so if your project still has a CONTEXT.md, rename it with git mv CONTEXT.md GLOSSARY.md, and a CONTEXT-MAP.md with git mv CONTEXT-MAP.md GLOSSARY-MAP.md.
- A dash in the Learn more column means there's no teaching article yet. That's fine: every command explains itself. Type it, or ask HQ "what does /adr do?" first.

#### The daily loop

The commands you'll use most days. The Daily Loop walks through the core rhythm.

| /startwork | Load your HQ context and surface the best next work options | The Daily Loop |

| /sync-registry | Rebuild a company's resource registry index | - |

##### Using HQ from Claude Cowork

These commands exist for one situation: you're running HQ inside Cowork (a sandboxed plugin host) where the normal HQ tools aren't directly reachable. They mirror the everyday commands above. All of them (ship in hq-pack-cowork).
| Command | Mirrors |
| /hq-cowork | The entry point: discovers and routes to every HQ capability available in Cowork |
| /hq-cowork-sync | /hq-sync |
| /hq-cowork-search | /search |
| /hq-cowork-files | /hq-files |
| /hq-cowork-share | /hq-share |
| /hq-cowork-secrets | /hq-secrets |
| /hq-cowork-dm | /dm |
| /hq-cowork-meetings | /meeting-notes and /signals |
| /hq-cowork-cli | Long-tail hq CLI functionality, safely guarded |
| /hq-cowork-install | Installs the Cowork pack itself |

#### Help

When something is broken, confusing, or missing.
| /setup | Run the guided setup wizard | Your First 30 Minutes |
| /tutorial | Hands-on lessons for HQ workflows | Getting More Help |
| /hq-checkup | Check that HQ is working and safely fix what it can, like updating HQ, starting the app, and backing up unsaved work | The "I'm Stuck" Guide |
| /hq-bug | File a bug report or feature request, with session context attached | Getting More Help |
| /hq-heal | Triage and repair HQ session errors like hook crashes or sync failures | The "I'm Stuck" Guide |
| /update-hq | Upgrade HQ to the latest release | FAQ |
| /free-disk-space | Find disk space you can get back from old worktrees, build folders, and dev caches. It only reports unless you add --apply, and it never deletes full repo copies, .env files, or work you haven't pushed | Storage and Disk Space |
| /cleanup | Audit and clean HQ structure, indexes, and stale content | - |
| /garden | Audit content for stale, duplicate, or inaccurate information | - |
| /knowledge-pulse | Run a freshness pass over company knowledge and policies | - |
| /harness-audit | Score your HQ setup across health and safety dimensions | - |
| /import-context | Bring your past AI work into HQ: Claude Code, Codex, Grok, and claude.ai history, plus skills, settings, and projects on disk. The old name /import-claude still works as an alias | - |
| /convert-codex | Add Codex support to an older, Claude-first HQ | - |
| /personal-interview | Build your owner profile and writing voice through an interview | - |

#### One thing this page doesn't cover

Slash commands run inside a session. The hq command you may see in terminal instructions is a different, smaller tool for managing packs and sync from outside a session. Capability Packs covers the part of it you're most likely to meet, and The HQ Ecosystem has the full product map.

#### If you get stuck

If a command on this page doesn't exist on your machine, check whether it's pack-tagged and see Capability Packs. If a command you read about elsewhere is missing, see The "I'm Stuck" Guide. Still stuck? /hq-bug.

## The HQ Rules — HQ

Source: https://hqforwork.com/hq-cheat-sheet

> Nine essential rules and three practical workflows for working in HQ.

#### Work in the HQ folder.

#### Tell HQ the outcome you want.

You do not need to memorize every command. Describe what you want to accomplish in plain language and HQ will guide you to the right workflow.

#### Share work so others can see it.

When you do work, that doesn’t automatically mean everyone can see it. Use /hq-share to give others permission to view it.
- /hq-share the report with [teammate] and give them read permission

#### Keep secrets out of chat and files.

Never paste API keys or passwords into a conversation or ordinary document. Store them in HQ Secrets, then grant access only to the people who need it.
- /hq-secrets

#### Deploy work people need to view.

Turn a document, report, deck, or app into a live link with HQ Deploy. Use the returned URL when you send the work to someone.
- /deploy

#### Start clean. Finish with a handoff.

Begin with a clear session. When the task is finished—or the session starts feeling slow or confused—leave a handoff and continue in a fresh session. Archive completed sessions only after the handoff.
- /startwork/handoff

#### Send the context, not just “done.”

Use HQ DM to tell a teammate what you shared, where the source file lives, and what you need from them. DMs reach people who share an active HQ company with you.
- /dm [teammate] and tell them the report is ready

#### Teach corrections. Report breakage.

If HQ needs to remember a correction or preference, teach it with Learn. If the product itself is broken, report it with HQ Bug.
- /learn [correction]/hq-bug [issue]

#### Invite new teammates through HQ.

Use the new-hire flow so identity, company membership, vault access, and the final connection check happen in the right order.
- /new-hire

#### Example workflows.

Each example shows both ways: use slash commands when helpful, or describe the whole outcome in one prompt.

##### Share a brief with the team

With slash commands:

As one prompt: “Deploy the brief, share it with my team, and send them a DM.”

##### Take a bigger project from idea to done

As one prompt: “For [company], help me brainstorm this project, make a plan, run it, then hand it off and sync the results.”

##### Hand work to another teammate

As one prompt: “Please hand this off, make sure it’s synced, share it with [teammate], and send them a DM letting them know it’s ready.”

[company], [prompt], and [teammate] are placeholders—replace them with the real values for your work.

## Install HQ on Mac or Windows — HQ Tutorial

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/tutorials/install-hq-macos

> Download HQ, sign in, and pick where your HQ folder lives. HQ installs in the background, then HQ Desktop opens a short guided setup.

Lesson 1 of 7 · HQ fundamentals

### Install HQ on Mac or Windows

Download HQ, sign in, and pick where your HQ folder lives. HQ installs in the background, then HQ Desktop opens a short guided setup.
**Written path**

8 steps

Contents
- Before you begin
- Download HQ
- Open HQ
- Sign in
- Choose where HQ lives
- Watch the two short explainers
- Start or join your company, if HQ asks
- Open HQ Desktop
- Start the guided setup
- Hit a snag?

#### Before You Begin

A Mac or Windows PC with permission to install apps. HQ isn’t available for Linux yet.

A Google or Microsoft account to sign in with.

A Claude account for Claude Code, or a ChatGPT account for Codex. You don’t need either one installed yet. HQ helps you sign in during setup.

#### Step-by-step walkthrough

Go to the HQ install page and click the download for your computer: Download for macOS on a Mac, or Download for Windows on a PC. Wait for it to finish.
- Go toOpen this place https://hqforwork.com/install Select Download for macOS or Download for Windows Expected

HQ.dmg (Mac) or the HQ setup .exe (Windows) is in your Downloads folder.
- Note

On Windows, your browser may hold the HQ setup file because it isn’t commonly downloaded. In Edge, open the Downloads panel, click the three dots on the file, choose Keep, then Show more and Keep anyway. In Chrome, open the file’s menu and choose Keep. In Firefox, right-click the paused file in the Downloads panel and choose Allow Download.

On a Mac, open HQ.dmg and drag HQ into your Applications folder, then open HQ from Applications. On Windows, run the HQ setup .exe from your Downloads folder. If Windows SmartScreen asks you to confirm, click More info, then Run anyway, and click Yes when Windows asks to make changes.
- Go toOpen this place Mac: drag HQ onto Applications, then launch HQ Windows: run the HQ setup .exe Expected

HQ opens full screen and says Everything you need. In one place.

Click Continue with Google or Continue with Microsoft. A browser window opens so you can sign in. Finish there and HQ picks up where you left off.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Continue with Google or Continue with Microsoft Expected

HQ shows It’s a folder and suggests where your HQ folder should live.

Joining a team? Sign in with the email your invite went to, so your team’s company shows up.

HQ keeps everything in one folder on your computer and keeps it in sync. The suggested spot works for most people, or click Choose… to pick your own. Then click Install here.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Install here Expected

HQ starts installing in the background. A small card in the corner shows its progress.

While HQ installs, two screens explain how it works: your folder stays on your computer while your team shares a company cloud, and one keyboard shortcut opens HQ from anywhere. Click Next on each, or Skip intro.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Next or Skip intro Expected

HQ shows Almost ready. while the install finishes, then HQ is ready.

Install usually takes a couple of minutes on a Mac. Windows can take a bit longer while antivirus scans run.

If you aren’t part of a company yet, HQ asks you to start one or join the company that invited you, then sign up free or request an enterprise demo. If you already belong to a company, HQ skips this screen.
- Expected

HQ shows HQ is ready.

Not ready to choose? You can also set up your team in the next part of setup.

On the HQ is ready screen, leave Share anonymous usage data ticked or untick it, then click HQ Desktop. HQ never collects your prompts or files, and you can change this later in Settings.
- ChoosePick this in HQ HQ Desktop Expected

HQ Desktop opens to a full-window setup screen.

Already use Claude Code or Codex? Their buttons sit under HQ Desktop on the same screen, so you can open your HQ folder there instead.

HQ Desktop asks you to name your HQ assistant. This assistant finishes setting up HQ with you and stays to help afterwards. Lesson 2 walks through every screen.

You see Name your HQ assistant.

#### You’re done when

HQ is installed, HQ Desktop is open, and you’re on the Name your HQ assistant screen.

#### Hit a snag? Here’s the fix.

**Q:** HQ won’t open

On a Mac, open HQ from your Applications folder, not from the disk image. HQ is signed and notarized by Apple, so macOS shouldn’t block it. On Windows, if SmartScreen or your antivirus stops the setup .exe, click More info, then Run anyway, or allow the app in your antivirus. If you still see a warning, reach out to support and we’ll fix it.

**Q:** Sign-in didn’t finish

Finish signing in in the browser window that opened. If you still see an error, click Continue with Google or Continue with Microsoft again. If it says a sign-in port is busy, close any other sign-in windows and try again.

**Q:** The install is taking a long time

The card in the corner shows what HQ is doing and how long it has been running, so you can see it’s still moving. On Windows, antivirus scans can slow it down. Leave the window open and let it finish.

**Q:** It says no coding tool is signed in

You’ll see this during setup in HQ Desktop. Click Sign in with your Claude account (for Claude Code) or Sign in with your ChatGPT account (for Codex) and finish in your browser. HQ notices on its own when you’re done. Lesson 2 shows the screen.

Something else going on? The HQ knowledge base walks through the most common fixes, or reach out and we’ll help you get unstuck.

## Set Up Your HQ Company and Team Workspace — HQ Tutorial

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/tutorials/set-up-hq-team-workspace

> Name your HQ assistant, choose your team, connect a coding tool, bring in your context, and find where your team’s shared files live.

Lesson 2 of 7 · HQ fundamentals

### Set Up Your HQ Company and Team Workspace

Name your HQ assistant, choose your team, connect a coding tool, bring in your context, and find where your team’s shared files live.
**Written path**

9 steps

Contents
- Before you begin
- Name your HQ assistant
- Choose your team
- Connect a coding tool
- Bring in your context
- Connect your note taker
- Connect your project tracker
- Meet your assistant
- Find your company’s folder
- Check your team in HQ Console
- Hit a snag?

#### Before You Begin

HQ is installed and HQ Desktop is open (see Lesson 1).

A Claude account for Claude Code, or a ChatGPT account for Codex. You only need one.

A few minutes to go through six short screens.

#### Step-by-step walkthrough

HQ Desktop suggests a name for your assistant. Keep it or type your own, then click Next: Your team. Names can include numbers but must start with a letter.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Next: Your team Expected

HQ asks Who do you work with?
- Note

The name shows up everywhere in HQ. You can rename your assistant later from its profile. Already have an assistant on another computer? HQ fills in its name for you.

Pick the company that invited you, click Start a company and type its name, or click Just me to keep HQ to yourself for now. Then click Next.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Start a company or Just me or pick the company that invited you Expected

Your company is joined or created, and HQ moves on to Your coding tools.

Starting a company makes you its owner. Chose Just me? You can add a company later.

Your assistant thinks with a coding tool signed in on your computer, under your own login. If Claude Code or Codex already shows Ready, click Next. If not, click Sign in with your Claude account (Claude Code) or Sign in with your ChatGPT account (Codex) and finish in your browser.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Sign in with your Claude account Next: Bring in your context Expected

At least one coding tool shows Ready, and Next takes you to Your context.

You sign in to the coding tool directly, so HQ never sees your password. One tool is enough.

HQ offers to read the tools you already work in on this computer, like your code folders and past Claude Code and Codex sessions, so your assistant starts out knowing your companies, projects and people. Click Bring it in, or Skip for now.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Bring it in or Skip for now Expected

HQ lists what it found, with a count for each source, then shows Next.

It reads only this computer, and nothing leaves it. It never reads passwords or keys.

If your company uses a meeting note taker like Fireflies, Otter or Read.ai, click Connect next to it and sign in, so your assistant can use what was said in meetings. Don’t use one? Click Next.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Pick your note taker or Next: Project management Expected

Your note taker shows Connected, or HQ moves on.

You only see this screen and the next one if you’re setting up HQ with a company.

If your team tracks work in a tool like Linear, click Connect next to it and sign in, so your assistant can see projects and tasks. Don’t use one? Click Next.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Pick your project tracker or Next: Done Expected

Your project tracker shows Connected, or HQ moves on to the last screen.

You can connect more apps later from Integrations.

The last screen sums up what you set up: your assistant, team, coding tool, context and apps. Click Talk to and your assistant’s name. It picks up the rest of setup in chat, starting after the steps you just finished.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Talk to [your assistant] Expected

Your assistant’s chat opens and it says hi by name. It doesn’t ask again about anything you already chose.

Want to invite a teammate? Just ask your assistant in the chat.

Click the folder icon at the top of HQ Desktop to open your HQ folder. Go into companies, then your company. Everything in there is shared with your team. The personal folder is just for you.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Click the folder icon (Open HQ folder) Expected

You can see your company’s knowledge, projects, policies, and skills folders.

Click the globe icon at the top of HQ Desktop. Pick your company, then open Team.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Click the globe icon (Open HQ Console) Expected

You’re listed as the owner, and anyone you invited shows as pending.

#### You’re done when

Your assistant has said hi by name, your company is in the sidebar, and HQ Console lists you as the owner.

#### Hit a snag? Here’s the fix.

**Q:** It says no coding tool is signed in

On Your coding tools, click Sign in with your Claude account (Claude Code) or Sign in with your ChatGPT account (Codex) and finish in your browser. HQ notices on its own when you’re done. If it says Sign in did not finish, click Try again.

**Q:** I want to skip the guided setup

Once you’re past Bring in your context, Continue in chat at the top takes you straight to your assistant’s chat, and it finishes setup with you there. You can also open your HQ folder in Claude Code or Codex and type /setup.

**Q:** Bring it in found nothing

That’s fine on a new computer. Your assistant learns as you work. Click Next to keep going.

**Q:** My team’s company didn’t show up

If a teammate invited you, sign in with the exact email the invite went to. HQ syncs your company by itself. If it can’t, you’ll see a banner with a Sync button.

**Q:** I chose Just me but now want a company

No problem. Ask your assistant to create a company, or run /onboard in Claude Code or Codex and choose create.

Something else going on? The HQ knowledge base walks through the most common fixes, or reach out and we’ll help you get unstuck.

## Store and Share API Keys with HQ Secrets — HQ Tutorial

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/tutorials/hq-secrets

> Save an API key with HQ’s secure form, choose who can use it, and share it without the key ever showing up in chat.

Lesson 3 of 7 · HQ fundamentals

### Store and Share API Keys with HQ Secrets

Save an API key with HQ’s secure form, choose who can use it, and share it without the key ever showing up in chat.
**Written path**

8 steps

Contents
- Before you begin
- Ask HQ for a safe place to put the key
- Paste the key into the secure form
- Check that HQ got it
- Choose who can use it
- Check the key in HQ Console
- Know who can use a secret
- Share related knowledge with the same group
- Check the final summary
- Hit a snag?

#### Before You Begin

HQ is signed in to a company that’s set up for your team (see Lesson 2).

You’re allowed to store the key and decide who uses it.

You have the API key handy to paste.

#### Step-by-step walkthrough

Tell HQ which API key your team needs. Don’t paste the key itself into the chat.
- PromptSend in your AI session I want to upload a [provider] API key for my team to use with HQ Secrets. Expected

HQ gives you a secure link to paste the key into. The link works once and expires after 24 hours.
- Note

Swap [provider] for the service you’re using, like HubSpot.

Open the link, paste the key, and click Submit. Don’t share the link in notes or chat.
- Go toOpen this place Open the link, paste the key, and submit Expected

The key is saved without ever showing up in your chat with HQ.

The key only ever shows up as dots, in the form and everywhere else in HQ.

Ask HQ to confirm the key arrived.
- PromptSend in your AI session Please validate you have received it. Expected

HQ confirms it has the key and asks who should be able to use it: one person, a group, or the whole company.

Share it with as few people as makes sense. This example makes a sales group. Use a name that fits your team.
- PromptSend in your AI session Create a new group called [group] and share it with [group]. Expected

HQ creates the group and gives it access to the key.

Swap [group] for your own group name.

In HQ Desktop, click Open HQ Console and go to Secrets. You’ll see the key listed, but not its value.
- Go toOpen this place Click Open HQ Console in HQ Desktop, then open Secrets Expected

The key is listed with who can use it, and the value stays hidden.

A company secret starts out private to whoever added it. You can share it with a person, a group, or the whole company, and choose whether they can read it, change it, or manage it. Personal secrets are yours alone and can’t be shared.
- Expected

You know who’ll be able to use a key before you share it.

If the group needs more than the key, like your sales playbook, share that with the same group too.
- PromptSend in your AI session Please share that API key with that group. Please share our [team] knowledge with that group. Expected

The key and the knowledge are shared with one group, so there’s one place to manage who has access.

Swap [team] for the knowledge you want to share. Only share what that group should see.

Read HQ’s summary. Make sure it names the right group and access, and doesn’t show the key.

The group is set up with access, and anyone added to it later can use the key without seeing it.

#### You’re done when

The key is stored, your group has access, and the key itself never showed up in chat.

#### Hit a snag? Here’s the fix.

**Q:** The secure link expired

Links work once and expire after 24 hours. Ask HQ for a new one, it only takes a second.

**Q:** A teammate can’t use the key

Check that they’re in the group you shared it with and signed in to HQ with the email that’s in your company. If they were added recently, have them run /hq-sync.

**Q:** I pasted a key into the chat by mistake

Treat that key as exposed. Create a new one at the provider, turn off the old one, and store the new one through the secure form.

Something else going on? The HQ knowledge base walks through the most common fixes, or reach out and we’ll help you get unstuck.

## Deploy a Private HQ App — HQ Tutorial

Source: https://hqforwork.com/getting-started/tutorials/hq-deploy

> Build a small web app with HQ, make it visible only to your company, and check that outsiders can’t get in.

Lesson 4 of 7 · HQ fundamentals

### Deploy a Private HQ App

Build a small web app with HQ, make it visible only to your company, and check that outsiders can’t get in.
**Written path**

6 steps

Contents
- Before you begin
- Describe the app
- Pick the company, if HQ asks
- Make it company-only
- Wait for it to go live
- Open it while signed in
- Make sure outsiders can’t get in
- Hit a snag?

#### Before You Begin

HQ is signed in to a company that’s set up for your team (see Lesson 2).

You know roughly what you want the page to show.

You know which company should own it and who should see it.

You can open a private or incognito browser window to test it.

#### Step-by-step walkthrough

Run /deploy and describe what you want. Stick to information that’s fine for your team to see, and don’t ask the page to show any API keys.
- CommandType exactly as shown /deploy Create a mini site that summarizes approved company information without exposing credentials. Expected

HQ starts building the app.

HQ usually knows the company from the folder you’re in. If you’re in more than one company, it shows you a preview and asks which one should own the app before it publishes anything.
- PromptSend in your AI session Deploy this to [company name]. Expected

The app belongs to the right company.
- Note

Swap [company name] for your company.

Tell HQ that only your company should be able to see it.
- PromptSend in your AI session Please make it company-only, so only members signed in to [company name] can see it. Expected

HQ locks the app so people have to sign in as a member of your company.

Keep the session open while HQ builds the app, shows you a preview, runs its safety checks, and publishes it.
- Expected

HQ tells you the app is live, only your company can see it, and it tested the sign-in page.

Open the link HQ gives you in your usual browser, where you’re signed in.
- Go toOpen this place Open the app link in your usual browser Expected

The app loads, and no API keys are visible.

The example page lists secret names, never their values. Keep it that way in your own apps.

Open a private browser window and go to the same link without signing in.
- Go toOpen this place Open the app link in a private browser window Expected

You get a sign-in page instead of the app.

#### You’re done when

Your teammates can open the app after signing in, a private window gets a sign-in page, and no API keys show up on the page.

#### Hit a snag? Here’s the fix.

**Q:** HQ deployed to the wrong company

Say “deploy this to [company name]” and run it again. Re-deploying the same project updates the same link.

**Q:** The page opens without asking anyone to sign in

Ask HQ to redeploy it company-only. Every link has exactly one access level, and public is the default.

**Q:** A teammate sees a sign-in wall they can’t get past

They need to sign in with the email that’s a member of your company. If they aren’t a member yet, invite them first.

Something else going on? The HQ knowledge base walks through the most common fixes, or reach out and we’ll help you get unstuck.

## Onboard a Team Member with /new-hire — HQ Tutorial

Choose Member or Admin. Pick Member unless they need to manage the company.
- ChoosePick this in HQ Select Member or Admin Expected

Your teammate gets the role that fits their job, and no more.

Admins can invite people and change access for the whole company, so save it for people who need that.
